## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89594.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89594.3.sa1)

This study aims to identify gene expression differences exclusively caused by cis-regulatory genetic changes by utilizing hybrid cell lines derived from human and chimpanzee. While previous attempts have focused on specific tissues, this study expands the comparison to six different tissues to investigate tissue specificity and derive insights into the evolution of gene expression.

One notable strength of this work lies in the use of composite cell lines, enabling a comparison of gene expression between human and chimpanzee within the same nucleus and shared trans factors environment. However, a potential weakness of the methodology is the use of bulk RNA-seq in diverse tissues, which limits the ability to determine cell-type-specific gene expression and chromatin accessibility regions. Their approach, using hybrid lines, naturally accounts for cell type heterogeneity avoiding the risk of false positives introduced by the otherwise confounding differences in cell type abundances between species, albeit the challenge of false negatives remains an issue. The authors now dully acknowledge this limitation in the manuscript.

Another concern is the use of two replicates derived from the same pair of individuals. While the authors produced cell lines from two pairs of individuals in a previous study (Agloglia et al., 2021). The reason for this experimental design is cost limitations. The authors now acknowledge that the use of replicates could enhance the ability to detect "more" species-specific changes in expression and chromatin accessibility. I would emphasize that replicates would increase robustness to the present findings, given that they are derived from a single pair of individuals.

Furthermore, the study offers the opportunity to relate inter-species differences to trends in molecular evolution. The authors discovered that expression variance and haploinsufficiency score do not fully account for the enrichment of divergence in cell-type-specific genes. The reviewer suggested exploring this further by incorporating external datasets that bin genes based on interindividual transcriptomics variation as a measure of extant transcriptomics constraint (e.g., GTEx reanalysis by Garcia-Perez et al., 2023 -- PMID: 36777183). The authors considered this question to be out of the scope of the paper, yet in my opinion this would enhance one of the main findings of this study.

Additionally, stratifying sequence conservation on ASCA regions, which exhibit similar enrichment of cell-type-specific features, using the Zoonomia data mentioned also in the text (Andrews et al., 2023 -- PMID: 37104580) could provide valuable insights. While the author did not find Zoonomia Phastcons values available, they used PhastCons derived from a 470-way alignment of mammals. I commend the authors for their diligent efforts, which undoubtedly bolster their findings that an enrichment in ASCA is evident across all levels of sequence conservation. However, this recent analysis indicates the presence of a potential relationship between sequence conservation and ASCA. It may be advantageous to consider evaluating more quantile subdivisions of maxZ values and pPhastCons values, with the inclusion of these results in the supplementary materials. This approach would be preferable, even if the precise reasons behind the observed discrepancy are not fully elucidated.

Another potential strength of this study is the identification of specific cases of paired allele-specific expression (ASE) and allele-specific chromatin accessibility (ASCA) with biological significance. Prioritizing specific variants remains a challenge, and the authors apply a machine learning approach to identify potential causative variants that disrupt binding sites in two examples (FABP7 and GAD1 in motor neurons). However, additional work is needed to convincingly demonstrate the functionality of these selected variants. Strengthening this section with additional validation of ASE, ASCA, and the specific putative causal variants identified would enhance the overall robustness of the paper. The authors have opted to defer these validations to future studies.

Additionally, the authors support the selected ASE-ASCA pairs by examining external datasets of adult brain comparative genomics (Ma et al., 2022) and organoids (Kanton et al., 2019). While these resources are valuable for comparing observed species biases, the analysis is not systematic, even for the two selected genes. For example, it would be beneficial to investigate if FABP7 exhibits species bias in any cell type in Kanton et al.'s organoids or if GAD1 is species-biased in adult primate brains from Ma et al. Comparing these datasets with the present study, along with the Agoglia et al. reference, would provide a more comprehensive perspective. In the revised version of the manuscript the authors have evaluated the expression of GAD1 in Ma et al, and FABP7 in Sousa et al 2017. For instance, GAD1 show cell type specific species biases in the later. The authors opted for not showing this in the manuscript, However, it remains unclear why certain datasets were favored over others, or why FABP7 should not be evaluated in Kanton et al.

The use of the term "human-derived" in ASE and ASCA has now been avoided.

Finally, throughout the paper, the authors refer to "hybrid cell lines." It has been suggested to use the term "composite cell lines" instead to address potential societal concerns associated with the term "hybrid," which some may associate with reproductive relationships (Pavlovic et al., 2022 -- PMID: 35082442). The authors have presented an eloquent and persuasive explanation that I found to be highly informative.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89594.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89594.3.sa2)

The authors utilize chimpanzee-human hybrid cell lines to assess cis-regulatory evolution. These hybrid cell lines offer a well-controlled environment, enabling clear differentiation between cis-regulatory effects and environmental or other trans effects.

In their research, Wang et al. expand the range of chimpanzee-human hybrid cell lines to encompass six new developmental cell types derived from all three germ layers. This expansion allows them to discern cell type-specific cis-regulatory changes between species from more pleiotropic ones. Although the study investigates only two iPSC clones, the RNA- and ATAC-seq data produced for this paper is a valuable resource.

The authors begin their analysis by examining the relationship between allele-specific expression (ASE) as a measure of species divergence and cell type specificity. They find that cell-type-specific genes exhibit more divergent expression. By integrating this data with measures of constraint within human populations, the authors conclude that the increased divergence of tissue-specific genes is, at least in part, attributable to positive selection. A similar pattern emerges when assessing allele-specific chromatin accessibility (ASCA) as a measure of divergence of cis-regulatory elements (CREs) in the same cell lines.

By correlating these two measures, the authors identify 95 CRE-gene pairs where tissue-specific ASE aligns with tissue-specific ASCA. Among these pairs, the authors select two genes of interest for further investigation. Notably, the authors employ an intriguing machine learning approach in which they compare the inferred chromatin state of the human sequence with that of the chimpanzee sequence to pinpoint putatively causal variants.

Overall, this study delves into the examination of gene expression and chromatin accessibility within hybrid cell lines, showcasing how this data can be leveraged to identify potential causal sequence differences underlying between-species expression changes.

All in all most conclusions appear solid, with the exception of the interpretation of a cell type/state identification machine learning model to pinpoint putatively causal variants. The described variants lack any functional validation and there is no data that measure the certainty of the results.

results.result: Six diverse cell types (motor neurons, cardiomyocytes, hepatocyte progenitors, pancreatic progenitors, skeletal myocytes, and retinal pigment epithelium) were successfully differentiated from human-chimpanzee hybrid iPSCs, representing diverse body systems. Successful differentiation was confirmed by expression of canonical marker genes and absence of pluripotency markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C6, C89, and C90 collectively demonstrate successful differentiation of six cell types from hybrid iPSCs. The expression of canonical markers (C6) and adequate sequencing depth (C90) provide strong evidence for successful differentiation. The experimental design with two hybrid lines and multiple replicates (C89) supports reproducibility.

results.result: RNA-seq samples clustered predominantly by cell type in hierarchical clustering, with human and chimpanzee alleles clearly separated by PC1 or PC2 within each cell type when using allelic counts. Within four cell type clusters, samples clustered by line rather than species.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, and C5 are supported by the clustering analyses shown in Figures 1b-d. The observation that samples cluster by line within cell types (C4) highlights the importance of measuring ASE to control for line-to-line variability, which strengthens the experimental design.

results.result: Thousands of genes with allele-specific expression (ASE) were identified in each cell type at FDR < 0.05, with most cis-regulatory divergence being cell-type-specific. Many more genes showed significant ASE in only a single cell type compared to genes with ASE in all cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, and C53 are well-supported by the data shown in Figure 2b and the UpSet plot. The identification of thousands of ASE genes with predominantly cell-type-specific patterns provides strong evidence for the main finding of cell-type-specific cis-regulatory divergence.

results.result: Cell-type-specific genes are enriched for ASE, and this enrichment is robust to different definitions of cell-type-specificity, FDR cutoffs, expression levels, and data splitting strategies. The enrichment persists when controlling for evolutionary constraint, suggesting that cell-type-specific genes and regulatory elements evolve faster than those shared across cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C14, C54, and C68 demonstrate a robust enrichment of ASE in cell-type-specific genes through multiple complementary analyses. The extensive robustness checks (different cutoffs, data splitting, constraint stratification) shown in supplementary figures strongly support this major finding. The conclusion that differences in constraint alone cannot explain the enrichment (C14) is well-justified.

results.result: Evidence for lineage-specific selection was detected in multiple cell types, with the most significant enrichments in motor neurons and cardiomyocytes. In motor neurons, genes involved in sodium ion transport and syntaxin binding showed coordinated chimpanzee-biased expression. In cardiomyocytes, the PPAR signaling pathway showed evidence of selection, including human-specific upregulation of NR1H3.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C23, C56, C69, and C99 collectively provide evidence for lineage-specific selection using a modified binomial test approach. The identification of functionally relevant pathways (sodium channels, syntaxin binding, PPAR signaling) in appropriate cell types strengthens the biological plausibility. The use of hybrid cells to control for environmental factors (C98) is a key strength. However, the functional consequences remain speculative without electrophysiology data (C118).

results.result: ATAC-seq data was generated from five cell types with an average depth of 184 million paired-end reads. After extensive filtering, 73,360-76,360 peaks were retained. Cell types clustered well by PCA, and species differences were clearly separated within each cell type.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 and C100 describe the ATAC-seq data generation and quality control. The discrepancy in the number of retained peaks (73,360 vs 76,360) between C25 and C100 is minor and likely reflects different stages of filtering. The clustering results support successful data generation.

results.result: TSS and promoter regions showed the least divergence in chromatin accessibility and strongest correlation between ASCA and ASE. Intriguingly, regions annotated as heterochromatin showed high divergence and correlations with ASE comparable to enhancers, particularly for distal heterochromatin CREs.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 present an unexpected finding about heterochromatin regions. The observation is well-supported by Figure 3d-e and supplementary figures. The distinction between proximal and distal heterochromatin CREs (C32-C33) adds important nuance. The clarification about chromHMM annotations (C102) is important for interpretation.

results.result: Cell-type-specific ATAC peaks are enriched for ASCA across all cell types. This enrichment is robust to different definitions of cell-type-specificity, various cutoffs, down-sampling to equalize sequencing depth, controlling for constraint on non-coding elements, and stratifying by number of SNPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 demonstrate enrichment of ASCA in cell-type-specific peaks through extensive robustness checks shown in multiple supplementary figures. The down-sampling analysis (C105) appropriately addresses the confounding effect of sequencing depth. The weak relationship between SNP number and ASCA (C106-C107) and the robustness when stratifying by SNPs (C37) address potential technical confounders.

results.result: Novel metrics (dEE and dCAE) were developed to quantify cell-type-specific differential expression and accessibility. Using these metrics, 154 peak-gene pairs with cell-type-specific ASE and ASCA were identified, with 95 showing concordant direction (more than expected by chance, p<0.005). This suggests tissue-specific cis-regulatory divergence in chromatin accessibility may often impact tissue-specific gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39, C57-C58, and C108 describe the development and application of novel metrics. The statistical test showing more concordant pairs than expected by chance (C39) supports a functional relationship. However, the interpretation that this divergence is 'neither necessary nor sufficient' (C108) appropriately acknowledges the complexity of gene regulation.

results.result: The FABP7 promoter shows human-biased ASCA and ASE specifically in motor neurons. Using the Sei deep learning model, two small indels were identified as likely causal variants, with a 1-base insertion introducing a GLIS2/3 binding site. FABP7 shows human-derived upregulation in several neuronal subtypes in published data. FABP7 plays a role in DHA uptake, which may contribute to neuronal survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44, C59-C60, C109-C110, and C121 present a detailed case study of FABP7. The integration of ATAC-seq, RNA-seq, Sei predictions, and published data provides converging evidence. The identification of specific indels (C43-C44) and the GLIS2/3 binding site provides a plausible molecular mechanism. However, the functional consequences remain speculative (C121) and would require experimental validation.

results.result: A putative enhancer near GAD1 containing a human accelerated region (HAR) shows chimpanzee-biased ASCA and ASE specifically in motor neurons. Sei analysis identified a single SNV (chr2:170,823,193) as the likely causal variant, predicted to disrupt binding sites for basic helix-loop-helix transcription factors. Analysis of hybrid and parental cortical organoids shows a developmental spike in chimpanzee GAD1 expression around day 50, consistent across GABAergic neuron subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C52, C61-C62, C111-C115, C122-C123 present a comprehensive case study of GAD1. The integration of ATAC-seq, RNA-seq, Sei predictions, hybrid organoid data, and published single-cell data provides strong converging evidence. The identification of a specific SNV in a HAR (C48-C49) and the developmental dynamics (C50-C52, C113-C115) are particularly compelling. The acknowledgment of uncertainty about functional consequences (C122) and need for further validation (C123) is appropriate.

results.result: Two PP hybrid2 samples showed slight chimpanzee bias likely due to contamination. A correction was applied that was validated by simulation to be conservative and not substantially affect log fold-change estimates.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 describe a quality control issue and correction. The simulation-based validation (C93, Figure 1—figure supplement 4) demonstrates that the correction was appropriate and conservative. This transparency about data quality issues and the validation of the correction method strengthens confidence in the results.

results.result: SKM showed fewer ASE genes than other cell types. All analyses were repeated with and without SKM, yielding qualitatively similar results.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 acknowledge a limitation with the SKM data and describe the robustness check performed. The fact that results were qualitatively similar regardless of SKM inclusion supports the robustness of the main findings. This is an appropriate handling of a potential data quality issue.

results.result: The neurotrophin family shows complex cell-type-specific ASE patterns. For example, NTRK3 is chimpanzee-biased in RPE but human-biased in MN, while NTRK1 is chimpanzee-biased in MN but human-biased in CM and SKM. This indicates complex cis-regulatory changes in the regulatory landscape of these genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C96, and C97 describe cell-type-specific ASE patterns in the neurotrophin family. The data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 supports these observations. This example effectively illustrates the complexity of cell-type-specific cis-regulatory divergence.

results.result: Changes in expression of cell-type-specific genes may be less deleterious than changes in broadly expressed genes, supporting the idea that cell-type-specific divergence may be less pleiotropic. However, it remains unclear whether positive selection or lower constraint plays a larger role in driving faster evolution of cell-type-specific genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C55, C116, and C117 present an interpretation of the enrichment results. The conclusion is appropriately cautious, acknowledging that the relative contributions of selection versus constraint remain unclear (C117). The interpretation is consistent with the data showing enrichment persists when controlling for constraint (C14), but additional work would be needed to definitively distinguish these mechanisms.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on human evolution, gene expression divergence, limitations of prior approaches, and advantages of the hybrid cell system and ATAC-seq for studying cis-regulatory divergence. The approach addresses many confounders inherent to interspecies comparisons and enables identification of specific regulatory elements underlying expression differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C88 provide background and context from the introduction. These claims accurately represent the state of the field and the rationale for the study. The advantages of the hybrid cell approach (C79-C83) and ATAC-seq (C86-C88) are well-established in the literature and appropriately cited.

results.result: The manuscript describes methodological approaches, acknowledges limitations, and proposes future directions. The computational pipeline was adapted from prior work. Hybrid cells are essential for determining genetic components of expression differences. The complexity of neuronal machinery makes functional predictions difficult without additional experiments. Future work could include additional assays, single-cell profiling, and integration with massively parallel reporter assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C91, C98, C118-C120, and C124-C126 describe methods, limitations, and future directions. These are appropriately acknowledged. The recognition that functional consequences require additional validation (C118, C123) demonstrates appropriate scientific caution. The proposed future directions (C124-C126) are reasonable extensions of the work.

results.result: CREs that are heterochromatic in some cell types may be more prone to large changes in accessibility during evolution, with significant impacts on cis-regulation of nearby genes. Large changes in accessibility of distal heterochromatin CREs may be particularly important in cis-regulatory evolution of ubiquitously expressed genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 present interpretations of the heterochromatin findings. These interpretations are consistent with the data shown in Figures 3d-e and supplementary figures. The distinction between proximal and distal heterochromatin CREs and their differential relationships with cell-type-specific versus ubiquitous genes adds important nuance to the interpretation.

results.result: Six cell types (motor neurons, cardiomyocytes, hepatocyte progenitors, pancreatic progenitors, skeletal myocytes, and retinal pigment epithelium) were successfully differentiated from human-chimpanzee hybrid iPSCs, representing diverse body systems. Samples clustered by cell type, species differences were clearly separated by PCA, and all cell types expressed canonical markers without pluripotency markers.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the study's methodological approach and data quality. One reviewer states the study 'expands the range of chimpanzee-human hybrid cell lines to encompass six new developmental cell types derived from all three germ layers,' and another notes 'the RNA- and ATAC-seq data produced for this paper is a valuable resource.' No concerns are raised about the differentiation success or cell type characterization.

results.result: Thousands of genes with allele-specific expression (ASE) were identified in each cell type, with most cis-regulatory divergence being cell-type-specific rather than shared across all cell types. Cell-type-specific genes and regulatory elements evolve faster than those shared across cell types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorse this as a primary finding. The editor states the study provides 'convincing evidence for enrichment of species differences in gene regulation in cell type-specific genes and regulatory elements.' One reviewer notes 'cell-type-specific genes exhibit more divergent expression' and describes this as a core finding that reviewers 'identify as key contributions.'

results.result: Cell-type-specific genes are enriched for ASE in the cell type where they are expressed, and this enrichment is robust across multiple definitions, FDR cutoffs, and controls for constraint. This suggests that changes in cell-type-specific genes may be less deleterious than changes in broadly expressed genes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. One reviewer summarizes that 'cell-type-specific genes exhibit more divergent expression' and notes the authors 'conclude that the increased divergence of tissue-specific genes is, at least in part, attributable to positive selection.' The robustness checks are not questioned.

results.result: Several signals of lineage-specific selection were detected in motor neurons and cardiomyocytes, including coordinated changes in genes involved in neuronal firing (sodium ion transporters and syntaxin binding proteins) and PPAR signaling pathway genes in cardiomyocytes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly highlight this as a key finding. The abstract states 'we identify several instances of lineage-specific natural selection that may have played key roles in specific cell types, such as coordinated changes in the cis-regulation of dozens of genes involved in neuronal firing in motor neurons.' One reviewer notes this as among 'the primary conclusions' that are convincingly supported.

results.result: ATAC-seq data from five cell types revealed patterns of allele-specific chromatin accessibility (ASCA). TSS and promoter regions showed the strongest correlation between ASCA and ASE, but intriguingly, regions annotated as heterochromatin, polycomb repressed, or quiescent showed correlations as strong as enhancers.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the ATAC-seq findings without challenge. One reviewer notes 'a similar pattern emerges when assessing allele-specific chromatin accessibility (ASCA) as a measure of divergence of cis-regulatory elements (CREs) in the same cell lines.' The heterochromatin finding is presented as an observation without reviewer critique.

results.result: Cell-type-specific peaks are enriched for ASCA across all cell types, and this enrichment is robust to different definitions of cell-type-specificity, controls for evolutionary constraint, and stratification by number of SNPs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this finding as part of the primary conclusions. The editor states the evidence provides 'convincing evidence for enrichment of species differences in gene regulation in cell type-specific genes and regulatory elements.' The robustness checks are not questioned by reviewers.

results.result: Using newly developed metrics (dEE and dCAE), 95 peak-gene pairs were identified with highly cell-type-specific concordant changes in accessibility and expression, more than expected by chance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this methodological contribution and its results. One reviewer notes 'the authors identify 95 CRE-gene pairs where tissue-specific ASE aligns with tissue-specific ASCA' and describes the metrics as improving 'the ability to identify matching cell-type-specific ASE and ASCA.' No concerns are raised about the statistical significance or methodology.

results.result: FABP7 shows human-biased ASCA in its promoter and human-biased ASE specifically in motor neurons. Machine learning analysis identified two small indels as candidate causal variants, with one introducing a GLIS2/3 binding site. FABP7 may play a role in neuronal DHA uptake and survival.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express significant reservations about the causal variant identification. One reviewer states 'the described variants lack any functional validation and there is no data that measure the certainty of the results.' Another notes 'additional work is needed to convincingly demonstrate the functionality of these selected variants.' While the ASE/ASCA patterns are accepted, the mechanistic claims remain unvalidated.

results.result: A putative enhancer near GAD1 (overlapping a human accelerated region) shows chimpanzee-biased ASCA and ASE specifically in motor neurons. Machine learning identified a single-nucleotide substitution as the likely causal variant disrupting transcription factor binding. GAD1 expression shows a developmental spike in chimpanzee neurons that is reduced in humans.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raise the same concerns as with FABP7. One reviewer explicitly states 'most conclusions appear solid, with the exception of the interpretation of a cell type/state identification machine learning model to pinpoint putatively causal variants. The described variants lack any functional validation.' Another notes the authors 'have opted to defer these validations to future studies,' indicating the evidence is incomplete.

results.result: The experimental design included two independently generated hybrid lines per cell type with at least two biological replicates each, sequenced to an average depth of 134 million paired-end reads. Contamination in PP hybrid2 samples was identified and corrected, with validation showing the correction was conservative.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the experimental design but note limitations. One reviewer states 'the study investigates only two iPSC clones' and emphasizes 'replicates would increase robustness to the present findings, given that they are derived from a single pair of individuals.' However, the data quality and contamination correction are not challenged, and reviewers accept the authors' acknowledgment of this limitation.

results.result: NTRK3 and NTRK1 show cell-type-specific differential expression patterns, with opposite biases in different cell types, indicating complex cis-regulatory changes in the neurotrophin pathway.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these specific examples. They are presented as supporting evidence for the broader finding of cell-type-specific divergence, which reviewers explicitly endorse.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on human evolution, the theoretical advantages of cell-type-specific cis-regulatory changes, the limitations of previous approaches, and the advantages of using hybrid cells and ATAC-seq to study cis-regulatory divergence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the study's conceptual framework and methodological approach. One reviewer states 'these hybrid cell lines offer a well-controlled environment, enabling clear differentiation between cis-regulatory effects and environmental or other trans effects.' The theoretical motivation is not challenged.

results.result: Hybrid cells are essential for determining that the human-specific upregulation of NR1H3 in cardiomyocytes has a strong genetic component, as NR1H3 expression is very responsive to environmental factors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorse the value of the hybrid cell approach. One reviewer notes the hybrid cells 'enable clear differentiation between cis-regulatory effects and environmental or other trans effects,' directly supporting this claim about NR1H3.

results.result: After filtering, 76,360 ATAC-seq peaks were retained. ChromHMM annotations reflect the most common chromatin state across cell types, not constitutive states. CREs that are heterochromatic in some cell types may be more prone to evolutionary changes, particularly for ubiquitously expressed genes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these technical details or interpretations. The ATAC-seq data quality and analysis are accepted as part of the overall convincing evidence for the study's conclusions.

results.result: Tissue-specific cis-regulatory divergence in chromatin accessibility may often impact tissue-specific gene expression, although this divergence is neither necessary nor sufficient to do so.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this nuanced interpretation. One reviewer notes the authors 'identify 95 CRE-gene pairs where tissue-specific ASE aligns with tissue-specific ASCA,' implicitly accepting that the relationship is not deterministic.

results.result: Broad changes in expression of cell-type-specific genes may be an important substrate for evolution, but it remains unclear whether positive selection or lower constraint plays a larger role. The complexity of neuronal machinery makes it difficult to predict functional effects without additional experiments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these limitations and uncertainties. One reviewer notes the authors acknowledge 'it remains unclear whether positive selection or lower constraint plays a larger role,' and reviewers do not challenge this honest assessment of the data's limitations.

results.result: Future directions include additional bulk assays (methylation, chromatin conformation, translation rate), deep single-cell profiling of multiple individuals, and integration with massively parallel reporter assays and deep learning models.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly support these future directions by noting current limitations. One reviewer states 'the use of bulk RNA-seq in diverse tissues...limits the ability to determine cell-type-specific gene expression' and another notes the need for 'functional validation,' aligning with the proposed future work.
